questions.q: State the definition of the definite integral \(\int_a^b f(x) dx\) as a limit of a sum using right endpoints. Write the expression for \(\Delta x\) and \(x_i\).
questions.a: The definite integral is \(\lim_{n\to\infty} \sum_{i=1}^n f(a + i\Delta x) \Delta x\) with \(\Delta x = \frac{b-a}{n}\). A wrong answer (e.g., using \(x_i = a + (i-1)\Delta x\) or omitting the limit) shows confusion between left/right endpoints or missing the limiting process that converts the approximation to an exact value.

questions.q: Explain why the limit of the Riemann sum \(\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i^*)\Delta x\) gives the exact area under \(y=f(x)\) for a continuous positive function, whereas any finite \(n\) only gives an approximation.
questions.a: For finite \(n\), rectangles either overestimate or underestimate the curved area; the error is the sum of small curved regions between the rectangles and the curve. As \(n\to\infty\), \(\Delta x\to 0\), the width of each error region vanishes, and the total error tends to zero. A wrong answer that says "rectangles become the curve" reveals a misunderstanding of the limiting process — the rectangles never become the curve; their total area converges to the area under the curve.

questions.q: Evaluate \(\int_0^2 (x^2 + 1) dx\) as a limit of a sum using right endpoints. Show all steps including the summation formulas.
questions.a:
\(\Delta x = \frac{2}{n},\; x_i = \frac{2i}{n}\).  
Sum = \(\sum_{i=1}^n \left[\left(\frac{2i}{n}\right)^2 + 1\right] \frac{2}{n} = \frac{8}{n^3}\sum i^2 + \frac{2}{n}\sum 1\).  
\(\sum i^2 = \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6},\; \sum 1 = n\).  
Sum = \(\frac{8}{n^3}\cdot\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} + \frac{2}{n}\cdot n = \frac{4}{3}\frac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{n^2} + 2\).  
Limit \(n\to\infty\): \(\frac{4}{3}\cdot 2 + 2 = \frac{8}{3}+2 = \frac{14}{3}\).  
A wrong answer often misapplies \(\sum i^2\) or forgets to multiply by \(\Delta x\) in the second term, showing algebraic carelessness.

questions.q: Compare the right-endpoint sum and the midpoint sum for \(f(x)=x^2\) on \([0,1]\) with \(n=4\). Which is larger? Why does the midpoint rule generally give a better approximation for the same \(n\)?
questions.a:
Right-endpoint: \(\Delta x=0.25\), \(x_i=0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0\); sum = \(0.25(0.0625+0.25+0.5625+1)=0.46875\).  
Midpoint: \(x_i^*=0.125,0.375,0.625,0.875\); sum = \(0.25(0.015625+0.140625+0.390625+0.765625)=0.328125\).  
Exact integral = \(1/3 \approx 0.3333\). Midpoint is closer because errors from over/under estimation cancel symmetrically. A student who says "right-endpoint is always larger" misses that for decreasing functions the opposite holds; the key is the symmetry of error.

questions.q: A student writes: \(\int_0^3 x^2 dx = \lim_{n\to\infty} \sum_{i=1}^n \left(\frac{3i}{n}\right)^2\). Identify the error and correct it.
questions.a: The student omitted \(\Delta x = \frac{3}{n}\) in the summand. The correct sum is \(\lim_{n\to\infty} \sum_{i=1}^n \left(\frac{3i}{n}\right)^2 \cdot \frac{3}{n}\). Without \(\Delta x\), the sum diverges to infinity. This error shows the student treats the sum as just function values, not areas of rectangles (height × width).

questions.q: Construct a function \(f(x)\) on \([0,1]\) and a partition with \(n=3\) such that the left-endpoint Riemann sum equals the right-endpoint Riemann sum, but the function is not constant. Explain why this happens.
questions.a: Example: \(f(x) = \sin(2\pi x)\) on \([0,1]\) with \(n=3\). Left endpoints: \(0, 1/3, 2/3\); right endpoints: \(1/3, 2/3, 1\). Both sums are zero because \(\sin(0)=\sin(2\pi/3)+\sin(4\pi/3)=0\) and similarly for right. The function is symmetric about the midpoint of each subinterval, so left and right samples cancel. A poor answer gives a constant function or cannot explain the cancellation, missing the role of function symmetry.
